expected_evidence: Geological: Ice-core and marine/lacustrine sediment cores dating Meltwater Pulse 1A (~14,600 BP) and 1B (~11,500 BP), including delta-O18 shifts, sea-level jump signatures, and abrupt cooling markers correlated in time with extinction horizons.

Geological/stratigraphic: Younger Dryas boundary layers (e.g., black mats) in North American sediment sequences marking abrupt climate reversal, cross-referenced against last-appearance stratigraphy of megafauna.

Material/paleontological: Radiocarbon-dated fossil remains of North American megafauna (mammoth, mastodon, horse, camel, ground sloth, short-faced bear) clustering their last-appearance dates around meltwater-pulse/Younger Dryas transitions, compiled in extinction chronology databases.

Genetic: Ancient DNA (including sedaDNA) from megafauna populations showing bottlenecks, declining genetic diversity, or population collapse timed to climate transitions rather than solely to human arrival.
Genetic: Phylogeographic reconstructions of megafaunal population size changes (e.g., mammoth, horse, bison) using coalescent/Bayesian skyline methods anchored to radiocarbon-calibrated timescales.

Astronomical/geochemical (tangential, competing-hypothesis adjacent): Any correlated proxy records (e.g., isotopic or geochemical anomalies) used to argue for vs. against a purely climatic mechanism as opposed to impact or overkill mechanisms.

Model-prior: General paleoclimatic and paleontological literature (not directly verified in this evidence set) suggesting debate between climate-driven, human-overkill, and multi-causal explanations for the North American megafaunal extinction.
response.rationale: The hypothesis's interval (-19050 to -9050) spans the tail of the Upper Paleolithic through the Younger Dryas into the early Holocene, straddling three detectability rows. Textual, linguistic, oral_tradition, and iconographic channels are essentially unavailable this deep in prehistory (0.0-0.25 across all three periods) and their absence is fully expected by detectability alone, not by falsity. However, the two evidence classes most relevant to this specific hypothesis — geological (0.6-0.65) and genetic (0.25-0.35) — are comparatively strong for this timescale, because meltwater pulses and Younger Dryas cooling leave robust, well-preserved physical signatures (ice cores, sediment stratigraphy, sea-level records) and because ancient/sedimentary DNA techniques have matured enough (as model-prior knowledge, unverified in the provided evidence text) to recover megafaunal population history over 10,000-20,000 year timescales. Material evidence (radiocarbon-dated fossil last-appearance data) is also moderately robust (0.35-0.45). Given that this is an actively studied topic in mainstream paleoclimatology/paleontology with a genuine record of ice-core, sediment, and aDNA-based chronological correlation work, I adjust detectability upward from the raw table average (~0.3) to about 0.55 for the geological+genetic+material composite that matters most here, reflecting that absence of textual/oral/iconographic evidence is fully explained by period constraints, while the core geological/genetic evidence needed to corroborate or refute a climate-driven mechanism is plausibly recoverable and has likely already been partially explored in the real scientific literature — though the causal 'corroborated' claim remains contested against competing overkill and impact hypotheses.
